To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transgenic mice expressing the ApoE variants ApoE4 (C112R) and/or ApoE4 L28P; C 112R exhibit a reduced motor activity and a reduced locomotor activity, respectively, in the absence morphological changes.
overexpression of the human ApoE4 transgene in the glial compartment of mice is not sufficient to produce a behavioral deficit.

the transgenic mice carrying ApolipoproteinE4(C112 R) and ApolipoprotenE4(L28 P; C112 R) were generated and that these mice did not show any differences in cognitive tests at one and a half years of age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation of transgenic mice that express human ApoE4 variants in order to study the influence of these variants on the development of Alzheimer's disease.
a detailed analysis of the transgenic mouse lines AD71 and AD61, and the comparison of their phenotype with that of wild-type mice.
the characterization of the ApoE transgenic mice and the development of an animal model for Alzheimer's disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transgenic mice are a good model to study the effects of ApoE variants on the brain and behavior but not to study Alzheimer's disease.
ApoE4 is not a sufficient cause for Alzheimer's disease, but that it is a necessary condition for the disease.
the ApoE isoform-specific effects are not simply due to the amount of protein produced but rather to a combination of protein amount and protein quality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ApoE genotype does not influence cognitive performance in the mouse.

ApoE4 transgenic mice may be used to study the effects of ApoE on the development of neurodegenerative diseases but that the results should be interpreted with caution and that the effects may be strain-dependent.
ApoE4 transgenic mice may not be the best model for studying the effects of the ApoE isoforms on Alzheimer's disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ApoE4 is a risk factor for the development of AD, but that it alone is not sufficient to produce AD-like pathology in mice.
ApoE4 transgene expression in the mouse does not lead to cognitive deficits, but may cause behavioral abnormalities.
the transgenic mouse models of ApoE are not a simple reflection of the human condition.
